chunks: And what Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from Ahmad ibn Ishaq and Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father, all of them from Bakr ibn Muhammad al-Azdi, who said:

I entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and with me was Ali ibn al-'Aziz. He said to me, 'Who is this?' I said, 'A mawla (client/freedman) of ours.' He said, 'Did you free him or his father?' I said, 'No, his father.' He said, 'This is not your mawla; this is your brother and cousin. Indeed, the mawla is the one upon whom the favor (of manumission) has been bestowed. So if it has been bestowed upon his father, he is your brother and cousin.'

key_terms.أَعْتَقْتُمُوهُ: Did you free him (referring to the manumission of the person himself)
key_terms.ابْنُ عَمِّكَ: Your cousin (son of your paternal uncle)
key_terms.النِّعْمَةُ: The favor (specifically referring to the act of manumission)
key_terms.مَوْلًى: Mawla (client/freedman, one who is under the patronage of another due to manumission)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between a mawla and a brother/cousin in Shia jurisprudence according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) distinguishes between the legal status of manumission and the resulting social kinship, ruling that if the father was freed, the son is considered a 'brother and cousin' rather than a 'mawla'. This clarification highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that the bond of manumission (*walā’*) is personal to the one who received the favor, thereby elevating the social standing of the freedman's descendants to that of close kinship (*akh wa ibn 'amm*).
